title: Metabolically Healthy Obesity Is Characterized by a Distinct Proteome Signature
coords: x and y are percent of the page image, measured from the top left
intro: International Journal of Molecular Sciences, March 2025.

hotspots.title: Question and result
hotspots.note: The authors compared 27 participants classified as having obesity only with 15 lean controls. Of 184 proteins measured, 24 differed between groups: 11 higher and 13 lower. The study did not track later disease.

hotspots.title: Figure 1: the study design
hotspots.note: Figure 1 shows the two groups and protein measurements. It labels the lean group BMI below 25 and the obesity group above 35.

hotspots.title: Table 1: who the groups were
hotspots.note: Table 1 begins here and continues on page 4. Mean ages were 36.4 and 38.8 years. The obesity group had higher weight, BMI, glucose, insulin and C-reactive protein, and a greater proportion of women: 17 of 27 versus 7 of 15.

hotspots.title: Figure 2A and 2B: the heatmap and volcano plot
hotspots.note: Each heatmap column is a person. On the volcano plot, each dot is a protein; right means higher in the obesity group, and up means a smaller p-value. IL-6 is near the top right.

hotspots.title: Figure 2C: the 24 proteins
hotspots.note: IL-6 has the largest increase (log2 fold change 1.17), followed by CXCL10 and CCL19. SIRT2 and AXIN1 have the largest decreases. The authors used a 1.25-fold change threshold and a false discovery rate below 0.05, adjusting for age, sex and race.

hotspots.title: Figure 3A: how the proteins relate
hotspots.note: The STRING network shows associations among the proteins. IL-6 and CXCL10 have the most links; the authors describe an inflammation cluster.

hotspots.title: Figure 3B and 3C: pathways
hotspots.note: In Figure 3B, green marks downregulated pathways such as regulation of T-cell differentiation; red marks upregulated pathways such as leukocyte chemotaxis. Figure 3C lists enriched molecular functions, including chemokine, cytokine and growth-factor activity.

hotspots.title: How the authors interpret it
hotspots.note: The authors discuss earlier links between these proteins, inflammation and insulin resistance. Their cross-sectional study cannot establish whether participants will develop disease.

hotspots.title: The authors' own limits
hotspots.note: The authors note the small cohort, single time point and unequal sex distribution. The discussion continues on page 9 with a call for a larger, multiethnic study followed over time.

hotspots.title: Figure 4: the authors' hypothesis
hotspots.note: The authors combine the protein results with earlier disease associations to propose possible links. This schematic does not show disease outcomes observed during follow-up.

hotspots.title: How the proteins were measured
hotspots.note: Olink uses pairs of DNA-tagged antibodies to measure relative protein abundance. The authors used two 92-protein panels and tested group differences with limma.

hotspots.title: Who did what
hotspots.note: The paper credits me and six co-authors with leading cohort sample collection, processing and ethical approvals. Other authors handled study design, analysis and writing.
